newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade election commission turns to higher court.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade election commission turns to higher court.

text.p: Belgrade's electoral commission on Sunday referred the disputed victory of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's socialist party in city elections in November to Yugoslavia's highest court.

Commission President Radomir Lazarevic told a news conference that the body had formally endorsed the contested results, which have sparked nearly three weeks of mass street protests in the Yugoslav capital.
This followed the decision by the Serbian Supreme Court on Saturday to reject an appeal by the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition accusing Milosevic's administration of vote fraud.
But Lazarevic said the commission had appealed to the Yugoslav Supreme Court, the Federal Public Prosecutor and the Serbian Public Prosecutor to reexamine this decision.

"This does not mean necessarily that we are right. This means that the rule of law does exist in this country and must be respected," he said. All three legal bodies must respond within 48 hours, he added.
Some observers said they believed Lazarevic's move was an attempt to buy more time for Milosevic, who is under increasing pressure by the West to respect the initial opposition victory.

But a senior opposition official said the move was aimed at scrapping the Belgrade elections altogether. Milan Bozic is political adviser to Vuk Draskovic, the leader of the Serbian Renewal Movement -- a partner in Zajedno.

"Our people tell us that Lazarevic is angry at the (Serbian) Supreme Court decision and will not verify nominations for the new Socialist deputies who won the seats in the city hall thanks to the Supreme Court ruling," he told Reuters.
"In that case, the city assembly cannot be constituted, the city will be left without a governing body and Milosevic will simply say he was forced to call new elections," Bozic said.
Zajedno claimed victory in Belgrade and another 14 of Serbia's biggest towns in the local elections on November 17.
The opposition said it had won more than 60 seats in Belgrade, wresting control of the capital from the left for the first time in 50 years.

But Milosevic's ruling Socialist Party (SPS), which dominates at the national level, and its ally, the Yugoslav United Left (JUL), said there had been voting irregularities and a Belgrade municipal court annulled the results in the capital.
The opposition then lodged a plea to the Serbian Supreme Court which was rejected on Saturday, angering tens of thousands of Zajedno supporters staging a mass protest in Belgrade.
Following the Serbian court's decision, Lazarevic announced the official results.
"SPS and JUL won 66 seats, Zajedno (opposition coalition) 32, Serbian Radical Party 10 and Democratic Party of Serbia two," he said.
